title: Replication
objective: Keep copies of the data on several machines, and handle the catches: stale reads, failover, and lost writes.

sources.title: PostgreSQL documentation: Log-Shipping Standby Servers (asynchronous shipping can lose recent transactions; synchronous replication)
Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O'Reilly, 2017): replication: leaders and followers, replication lag, failover

simplifies: One leader and two followers; each copy arrives after the lag slider's delay (give or take 30%); a failure is noticed after 1 second and the most up-to-date follower is promoted. Real systems also deal with split brain (two leaders at once), network partitions and picking which writes to keep. Numbers are illustrative.

challenges.title: Stale reads
challenges.prompt: Reads go to followers that are 300 ms behind. Keep stale reads at 1% or less for 10 seconds.

predict.prompt: Someone saves a change and reloads at once. The read goes to a follower 300 ms behind. What do they see?

options.explanation: Right. The follower hasn't received the change yet, so it can return the old version.
Only copies that have received the write can show it.
Followers still answer; they may just be behind.

challenges.hint: Which copy always has the latest confirmed write?
challenges.explain: The leader has every confirmed write, so reading from it is never stale. The trade-off: the leader now does all the reading too. Real systems often read from the leader only when it matters (for example, right after your own write).

challenges.title: Leader crash
challenges.prompt: The leader will crash 3 seconds in. Keep failed writes at 1% or less for 8 seconds after that.

predict.prompt: Only the leader accepts writes. When it crashes, what happens to writes?

options.text: They fail until another copy becomes leader
options.explanation: Right. Followers don't take writes until one of them is promoted.

options.text: A follower takes them straight away
options.explanation: Only after it has been promoted to leader.
Without a leader, there is nowhere to write.

challenges.hint: Something has to notice the leader is gone and promote a follower.
challenges.explain: With automatic failover, the failure is noticed and the most up-to-date follower is promoted, so writes resume after a short gap.

challenges.title: Don't lose writes
challenges.prompt: Writes are confirmed before they are copied (asynchronous), with 500 ms of lag. The leader crashes 3 seconds in. Lose no confirmed writes for 10 seconds.

predict.prompt: The leader confirmed some writes but hadn't copied them yet when it crashed. After failover, what happens to them?

options.text: They are lost: the new leader never got them
options.explanation: Right. Confirmed but not copied means only the dead machine had them.
It can't recover what it never received.
The only machine that had them is gone.

challenges.hint: What if a write were only confirmed once at least one follower had a copy?
challenges.explain: With synchronous copying, a write is confirmed only after a follower has it, so promoting the most up-to-date follower keeps every confirmed write. The cost shows in "Write wait": every write now waits for the lag.

options.text: How far behind the leader a follower is
options.explanation: Right. Changes take time to reach each copy, so followers can be behind.
Lag is about the copies falling behind, not the leader's speed.

options.text: The time to restart a server
options.explanation: That is recovery time, a different thing.

quiz.prompt: Synchronous replication avoids losing confirmed writes. What does it cost?

options.text: Every write waits for a follower to confirm, so writes are slower
options.explanation: Right. Safety for speed: the write isn't done until a copy has it.
The write has to wait for the network round trip to a follower.
It makes data safer; stale reads come from reading lagging followers.
